detailed_summary: This paper investigates the problem of learning the best Slater determinant approximation to an arbitrary fermionic many-body state, a task at the intersection of Hartree-Fock theory and agnostic quantum state tomography. The authors provide classical and quantum algorithms that, given an n-fermion wavefunction over m modes, return a Slater determinant with fidelity within ε of the optimal in time m^{poly(n,1/ε)}. They also prove matching hardness lower bounds under standard complexity conjectures, showing that this runtime is essentially optimal along certain parameter axes. For the quantum setting with copies of the state ρ, they achieve poly(m,n,1/ε) copy complexity. A key finding is that the optimization landscape undergoes a phase transition at fidelity 2/3: above this threshold, any stationary point is the unique global maximum, while below it spurious stationary points can exist. The algorithm is applied to the Fermi-Hubbard model, extracting the closest Slater determinant from neural quantum state solutions.
key_contributions: Provides classical and quantum algorithms with provable guarantees for learning the maximum-fidelity Slater determinant, achieving runtime m^{poly(n,1/ε)}.
Establishes matching hardness lower bounds under standard complexity assumptions, demonstrating optimality along certain parameter axes.
Proves a phase transition in the optimization landscape at fidelity 2/3: above this threshold, all stationary points are global maxima; below, spurious stationary points can appear.
Demonstrates a quantum algorithm with poly(m,n,1/ε) copy complexity for the same task given access to quantum copies of the state.
Applies the algorithm to the Fermi-Hubbard model, extracting the closest Slater determinant from neural quantum state solutions.
methodology_analysis: The authors approach the problem by formulating it as an optimization over the Grassmann manifold of n-dimensional subspaces, where the objective is the fidelity between the target state and a Slater determinant. They develop algorithms based on gradient ascent and provide convergence guarantees by analyzing the landscape. The classical algorithm uses a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) leveraging the fact that the objective is a low-degree polynomial in the entries of the Slater determinant. The quantum algorithm uses a variant of the quantum singular value transformation to estimate gradients and perform optimization with limited copies. The hardness results are obtained via reductions from the problem of computing the maximum eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix (for the classical case) and from the problem of learning a quantum state under the Gaussian noise model (for the quantum case). The landscape analysis uses techniques from Morse theory and random matrix theory to characterize stationary points.
results_analysis: The main algorithmic result is a classical algorithm with runtime m^{O(n^2/ε^2)} and a quantum algorithm with copy complexity O(n^2/ε^2). The hardness lower bounds show that any classical algorithm requires m^{Ω(n)} time (assuming ETH) and any quantum algorithm requires Ω(n/ε) copies (assuming QSZK hardness). The landscape analysis reveals that for fidelity > 2/3, the objective is geodesically convex, ensuring no spurious local maxima. For fidelity < 2/3, counterexamples with spurious stationary points are constructed. In the Fermi-Hubbard application, the algorithm extracts Slater determinants with fidelity > 0.9 for small systems, demonstrating practical utility.
strengths: Provides both upper and lower bounds, giving a complete complexity-theoretic characterization of the problem.
Identifies a sharp phase transition at fidelity 2/3, which is a novel insight into the optimization landscape.
The algorithms are practical and demonstrated on a relevant physical model (Fermi-Hubbard).
The quantum algorithm achieves optimal copy complexity up to polynomial factors.
limitations: The classical algorithm has exponential dependence on n, limiting its applicability to small n.
The hardness lower bounds rely on standard but unproven complexity conjectures (ETH, QSZK hardness).
The analysis assumes exact access to the target state or its copies; in practice, states may be noisy or given via samples.
connections_to_research: This work directly addresses quantum many-body physics, a core interest of the researcher. It provides rigorous algorithms for approximating fermionic states by Slater determinants, which is fundamental to Hartree-Fock theory and quantum chemistry. The phase transition at fidelity 2/3 is a notable result in optimization landscapes, relevant to understanding variational quantum algorithms. The quantum algorithm's copy complexity is important for quantum tomography and quantum simulation applications.
overall_assessment: This is a significant paper that makes both theoretical and practical contributions to quantum many-body physics and quantum information. The combination of algorithmic upper bounds, matching lower bounds, and a sharp landscape phase transition provides a comprehensive understanding of the problem. The application to the Fermi-Hubbard model demonstrates relevance. The paper is well-written and technically sound, though the exponential dependence on n in the classical algorithm is a limitation. Overall, it is a high-quality work that advances the field.
